134: Falla: as a falla monument that will be displayed from 15 to 19 March; they are divided into large and children's fallas. Fallas are classified by section. The Mascletà takes its name from the famous Masclets (firecrackers of great sound power). The name 'Masclet' derives from the qualifier 'mascle', which in Valencian means male and also brave.

The 'mascles' of the late 18th century involved throwing firecrackers at their feet and betting on who could withstand the most by stopping them with their feet. The one who held out against the most was the 'més mascle' (the most valiant), and that is where this pyrotechnic event gets its name.

Over time, masclets began to be tied with strings and connected to each other through fuses, so they could all be fired in sequence. In the 'Trams de Tro' (thunder stretches) it was very common for men to run beneath the Masclets as if accompanying the fire, taking part and maintaining that reputation as 'mascles' (valiant) that preceded them.

Ancient legends tell that in the times when Valencia was an Arab city, it was believed that if bats flew over the city, it would always remain their property.

In 1238, the year of the Reconquista, it was precisely a bat that changed the religious course of the city — a course that endures to this day.

During the siege of the ancient 'Balansiya', while the army of King James I slept, an enemy group infiltrated the camp with the intention of killing the king.

Good fortune willed that a bat flying in the vicinity collided with a drum and woke the troops with the din, an act that would prevent the incursion and achieve the capture of the city.

After this 'miracle' the king paid tribute to the animal and symbolised it at the top of the coat of arms.

It is true that bats have always been of great help, like swallows or swifts, for eating mosquitoes and other flying insects, thus preserving the wellbeing of citizens.

The origins of the Iglesia de Santa Catalina Màrtir date back to the reconquest of Valencia itself in 1238.

Following the reconquest and subsequent change of religion in the city, James I sought to reorganise the urban space.

To this end, he granted ownership of all Muslim mosques and cemeteries to the archbishopric, which in turn Christianised these temples by renaming them as parishes dedicated to saints of the new religion that would be established in these lands.

In May 1239, just one year after the reconquest, the Parish of Santa Catalina became one of the ten founding parishes of the city.

It should also be noted that the seizure of the mosques was not merely an instrument of Christianisation and ecclesiastical control over neighbourhood life, but also an instrument of administrative and political organisation; in fact, the town council was formed, in part, by the various parishes of the city.

The Portal de la Valldigna was built over the Arab city wall itself.

It served as an entrance to the Moorish quarter from the year 1400, when the gate was removed and the portal remained as it is preserved today.

The semicircular arch, built in ashlar masonry, was restored in 1965.

Above the arch, a reproduction of the original altarpiece can be seen — the original was placed at this very spot in 1589.

The altarpiece depicts King James II of Aragon, known as the Just, in the act of founding the Monastery of the Valldigna, whose name literally means worthy lands.

515:
In the 11th century, after the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba, the ancient Empire was divided into small factions known as Taifas.

Valencia, or Balansiya as it was known in Muslim times, was the capital of one of those Taifas. As a consequence, it experienced significant urban growth.

The increase in population and the constant attacks from North Africa prompted the inhabitants to expand the old city and its defensive perimeter.

The design of the new wall would transform Valencia and establish a new boundary.
516:
It was built with concrete and filled with stones of various sizes.

The wall allowed the inhabitants of Balansiya to resist the fierce siege by Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, better known as El Cid Campeador, in the year 1094, although it did not prevent the conquest.

The city was taken by the Christians, and so it remained until 1144, at which time Valencia passed once again into Muslim hands.

Throughout all this time, one thing did not change: the walls with their towers stood firm.
517:
Even after the Christian reconquest in 1238 by James I the Conqueror, the Arab wall was not destroyed; instead it was maintained as a protective measure for a century and a half.

This perimeter, of which visible remains can be seen today, had seven main gates and towers strategically placed every 25 metres.

The tower you can see right now has a semicircular plan and is built in rubble masonry.
518:
What is rubble masonry? It is a mixture of stones and mortar — a traditional cement made of lime, sand and water, to which clay and straw could also be added to increase its hardness.

Rubble masonry is a rough construction method that minimises material waste and is very well suited to tall structures.

The new Christian city surrounded the Arab one with a 4-kilometre wall, isolating the converted Muslims in a ghetto within its walls.

The Mudejars — or Sarraïns as they were known in Valencia — were Muslims who, in exchange for a substantial tribute, continued to live true to their faith.

It is worth noting that in the city of Valencia the three Abrahamic religions coexisted: Christian, Arab and Jewish.

Despite having different religious beliefs, a policy of agreements and mutual recognition in the interest of the city's progress was commonplace.

Their approach to urban planning was: houses first, then streets — the opposite of the Roman system, which built streets first and then houses.

As a result, the irregular layout is formed by houses that expand and encroach on adjacent streets, altering their course, even blocking streets and creating dead ends.

This monument, visitable today, was one of the first civilian shelters to be built during the Spanish Civil War, which took place from 1936 to 1939.

Due to the evolution of warfare, anti-aircraft shelters were essential to protect the population from enemy attacks and bombardments.

This particular one was built in 1937, the year in which Valencia served as the capital of the Spanish Republic.

The old wartime bunker could accommodate around 400 people inside.

In this space that once safeguarded the lives of many Valencians, today a museum allows us to witness a remarkable collection of artefacts from the era, as well as a photographic record reflecting day-to-day life amid the bombardments and misery.

All these historical records and manuscripts reflect how Valencia would look following the loss of thousands of human lives and the destruction of some of its historical monuments at the end of the Civil War.

Corpus Christi is the Catholic feast day celebrating the Eucharist; in it the sacrament of bread and wine is celebrated, with a special remembrance of the death and resurrection of Jesus.

Its primary purpose is to proclaim and strengthen the faith of believers.

Beyond its purely Catholic meaning, for Valencian society Corpus Christi is a demonstration of the coexistence of the festive and religious spirit.

The city pays tribute 60 days after Easter Sunday in the event known as the Fiesta Grande.

She is recognised by her white tunic and a white handkerchief that completely covers her face.

The Casa de las Rocas was built between 1435 and 1447 by order of King Peter IV, known as the Ceremonious.

Due to its proximity to the river, it has suffered numerous floods from each overflowing; which led to the building deteriorating constantly.

Fortunately, this was resolved after the diversion of the river, which gave rise to the beautiful park we will continue exploring throughout this Adventure.

This ancient two-storey house was also the residence of the Chaplain of the Rocas, who was responsible for their custody.

The house is entered through a tall lintel doorway, above which a triangular pediment can be found. Inside, there is an inner courtyard covered by a wooden-beamed roof.

After its restoration in 1980, a large balcony overlooking the inner courtyard was added to the upper floor.

Years later, following a well-deserved museographic renovation, explanatory panels, audiovisual screens and the division and naming of the various rooms were included.

535:
The Iglesia del Carmen had its beginnings in 1280. At that time, a modest house with a garden run by the Carmelite Order occupied this space. This would be the origin of the future Convent of Carmen.

After an initial expansion, the first church was consecrated in 1343 and has undergone gradual renovations since then.

A Gothic cloister with pointed arches, the large refectory or friars' dining hall, and the chapter house are clear examples that remain from its medieval past.

In 1555, the chancel — the area around the altar — was remodelled using the traditional vaulting system of a star-shaped ribbed vault.

Later, a second Renaissance cloister was built, but the most visible elements correspond to the Baroque period.

In 1613, work began on the façade-altarpiece of the temple, and in 1628 a new renovation lasting nearly 30 years was undertaken, renewing the interior in the Baroque taste of the time (1655).

This extravagant façade is considered one of the finest Mannerist altarpieces in the city.

Mannerism is an artistic style used at the end of the 16th century that focused on the alteration of order in architectural elements, tending towards unreality.

The façade altarpiece before you was created in two phases.

In the ancient Muslim Balansiya, cats were venerated.

History tells us that even Muhammad cut a piece of his tunic so as not to wake his cat, which had fallen asleep beside him.

Such was the veneration that they were considered pure beings.

This representation alludes to the four cats that survived following the conquest by Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, better known as El Cid Campeador.

The "Silk Road" was a network of trade routes dating back to the 2nd century BC.

It spread across the Asian continent and became established in Europe in the 15th century in the Hispanic kingdoms and the western Mediterranean; therefore, the silk industry was an activity that, even in Muslim times, was of great importance and enjoyed enormous prestige throughout Al-Andalus.

Given its location, the city of Valencia in the era of Al-Andalus was already renowned for its silk workshops.

By the 14th century there were already local silk weavers, predominantly Jewish, but it was from the 15th to the 18th century that Valencia's leadership as the main centre of Spanish silk was indisputable; in fact, the cultivation of the mulberry tree preceded that of the orange tree throughout the region.

The silk industry was one of the most powerful in the city, at one point boasting more than 3,000 looms.

Today, the Fallera dress keeps the silk craft alive in traditional hand-operated looms.

For the costume, between 10 and 15 metres of silk in more than 20 colours are used, as well as silver and gold thread.

An ancient tradition of the city's carpenters who, on the eve of their patron saint's feast day, burned old and useless odds and ends in the public squares, along with the leftover wooden odds and ends from their work.

Initially, the Falla consisted of bonfires of combustible materials that gradually evolved into the monuments we can see today.

The Fallas have become a very important tourist attraction because, in addition to being listed as a Festival of International Tourist Interest, in November 2016 UNESCO inscribed them on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The ancient Palau del Real was initially built in the 9th century as an Almunia — a Muslim recreational estate where the Sultans of the Taifa of Balansiya would retreat to rest.

This continued throughout the period of Christian conquest, and it was in the 14th century that it began to be rebuilt to become the palace of the Kings of the Crown of Aragon during their stay in the Kingdom of Valencia.

The palace was known as "the Palace of the 300 Keys", in reference to the number of rooms it once had.

In 1810, the ancient palace was dismantled by the Valencians for strategic defence reasons, in view of the possibility that it could become a stronghold for the invading troops of Napoleon.

Today, visible vestiges remain that mark the central lanes of certain stretches of the Jardí del Túria and the famous Jardins del Real, which at the time occupied a small part of what were once the Palace Gardens.

The magnificent building we see today dates from 1758, the final year of the reign of Charles III.

The building occupies a large rectangular block; its façades are composed of exposed brick walls between stone pilasters and straight and curved balconies on the first floor.

Above, the cornice with balusters, torch ornaments and empty niches displays the Baroque taste.

The works were begun by the Valencian academic Felipe Rubio Mulet, but he died before seeing it completed; it was his brother-in-law who finished the work in 1802.

Originally, this building was constructed as a Customs House.

It was the place through which all sea-borne trade was channelled, making Valencia one of the economic centres of the 18th century.

Although this space goes back even further in time, ancient chronicles from 1626 already mention a first customs house situated on this very spot, beside the city walls and the ancient city gate known as the "Puerta de la Mar".

The Church of Sant Joan de l'Hospital retains echoes of those transformations.

The historic complex has marked Arab influences in its rectangular plan, typical of the Mudéjar style.

An extension, this time in the Gothic style, was carried out in 1316.

The funerary hospital chapel was probably the first manifestation of ogival art in 13th-century Valencia.

The Church of Sant Joan de l'Hospital was declared a National Artistic Monument in 1943.

In 1936, at the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War, the building was set on fire on successive occasions and was destroyed, with the exception of part of the chapel, which remained burning for three consecutive days.

In these fires, nearly 13,000 written volumes and the Diocesan Museum with all the works of art inside were lost. The current building, in an eclectic style, was reconstructed between 1941 and 1946.

VIV14: A child is much more than a decorative element — it is a symbolic work representing the human relationship with water. Situated in an environment historically connected to irrigation and the orchard, it recalls the essential importance of water as the foundation of life, without which neither agriculture nor cities would exist. The composition reinforces this message: water symbolises the origin of life, the mother represents care and protection, and the child continuity and the future.
